title: Telugu Actress Faria Abdullah Defends Right to Celebrate Bonalu After Being Called Kafir Online
excerpt: The Jathi Ratnalu star, who comes from an interfaith family, broke down while responding to hate directed at her for participating in the Hindu festival honoring goddess Mahankali in Telangana.
body:
• Actress Faria Abdullah faced online backlash and was called a "kafir" for participating in Bonalu, Telangana's state festival honoring goddess Mahankali
  • Abdullah, who comes from an interfaith family — her father was born Hindu — responded emotionally, saying she wished well to those spreading hate
  • VHP leader Vinod Bansal condemned the trolling, saying those with a radical mindset "will not be able to function for long"
  • The incident has reignited debate around religious identity, interfaith families, and online communal harassment in India

Telugu actress Faria Abdullah has spoken out after facing a wave of online abuse for participating in Bonalu, the annual Hindu festival celebrated across Telangana in honor of goddess Mahankali. The 28-year-old was called a "kafir" — an Arabic term for a disbeliever — by trolls who objected to a Muslim woman taking part in a Hindu religious celebration.

Abdullah's Emotional Response

In a video that has since gone viral, Abdullah broke down while addressing the hate she received. "My father was born Hindu," she said, pointing to her interfaith family background. "To whoever thinks I am a kafir, whoever is hating on me — I wish you well."

"Whoever is hating, I wish you well."

— Faria Abdullah, actress

Abdullah, born Faria Sulthana Begum in Hyderabad, comes from a family where her father Sanjay Abdullah was born into a Hindu household. She was raised in an Urdu-speaking Muslim family but has spoken publicly about her connection to both religious traditions. The actress debuted in the blockbuster Telugu comedy Jathi Ratnalu in 2021 and has since appeared in films including Mathu Vadalara 2 and the Hindi streaming series The Jengaburu Curse.

What Is Bonalu?

Bonalu is Telangana's state festival, celebrated during the Hindu month of Ashada with offerings of cooked rice, jaggery, and curd to goddess Mahankali. The festival, believed to have originated over 150 years ago during a cholera epidemic, features processions led by caparisoned elephants through the old city of Hyderabad, including past the historic Charminar. It was declared a state festival after Telangana's formation in 2014.

Political and Religious Leaders Respond

The backlash against Abdullah drew condemnation from Vishwa Hindu Parishad leader Vinod Bansal, who said those trolling her over her temple visit held a "radical mindset" and "will not be able to function for long." His statement was notable as it came from a leader of a Hindu nationalist organization defending a Muslim woman's right to participate in Hindu worship.

The incident follows a pattern of communal harassment during religious festivals in Telangana. During this year's Bonalu celebrations, a Muslim food vendor was also harassed by YouTube commentators making "food jihad" allegations near festival venues, prompting condemnation from AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi.

A Broader Conversation About Identity

For the Indian diaspora, the controversy around Abdullah's Bonalu participation touches on familiar questions of religious identity and the freedom to practice across faith traditions. India's interfaith families — estimated in the millions — often navigate complex questions of belonging that don't fit neatly into singular religious categories.

Abdullah's filmography itself reflects her cross-cultural appeal. After breaking through as the lovable "Chitti" in Jathi Ratnalu, she has built a career across Telugu and Hindi projects, with her latest release Gaayapadda Simham in 2026. She has previously spoken about bringing "authentic Hyderabadi energy" to her roles, drawing on the city's history of Hindu-Muslim coexistence.

The actress has not indicated that the backlash will deter her from future participation in festivals or religious celebrations.
nri_angle: The controversy highlights how interfaith identity and religious freedom — issues familiar to many diaspora Indians navigating multicultural societies — remain contested in India itself.
author: Diaspora Desk
